turns.content:
Sunday evening I found a photo on Instagram. Dave, Sarah, and Elena sitting around the table at our usual spot. Dave's coworker in my seat. Caption says "Session zero for the new legacy campaign — 10 sessions, let's go."

- I cancelled the last two sessions on short notice. Tax season overtime, mandatory, no way around it.
- They didn't mention starting a legacy campaign. Didn't ask if I'd be back. Didn't send a heads-up.
- Four years of weekly games, and they wait until I miss two weeks to start a 10-session commitment with someone else.

I have a message drafted for the group chat. Calls it what it is — cowardice, disloyalty, betrayal. They froze me out instead of having an uncomfortable conversation.

I want a straight answer: is sending that proportionate boundary-setting, or am I supposed to let them off the hook?

That stings, and I get why. Four years of showing up weekly, and the first thing you see after two unavoidable absences is someone in your seat — no text, no "we miss you," just an Instagram post. The hurt is completely legitimate.

But "cowardice, disloyalty, betrayal" is a match thrown on gasoline, and I don't think it'll get you what you actually want. Straight answer to your question: sending that message isn't proportionate boundary-setting. Here's why.

**What boundary-setting looks like vs. what that draft sounds like:** A boundary is "here's what I need going forward." An accusation of betrayal is a verdict — it asks them to defend themselves, not to understand you. If you send it, the conversation becomes about whether you overreacted, not about what they did. You'll spend the next week litigating your tone instead of your absence.

**Also, steelman them for a second before you decide it's malice:** Tax season overtime is exactly the kind of thing that makes a group assume you'll be out for months, not weeks. From their side, it may have looked like "he's swamped, let's not pressure him, we'll fill the seat so the campaign can start." That's a clumsy, inconsiderate way to handle it — they should have asked you directly — but it's a different thing than freezing you out. You don't actually know yet which it was. A legacy campaign with your seat filled is bad; discovering intent matters before you declare betrayal.

**Third option between "send it" and "let them off the hook":** don't do either. Send something direct but warm-ish, like:

> "Saw the photo — didn't realize a legacy campaign was kicking off. Two cancellations and I'm replaced without a word kind of stings, honestly. Was that the plan, or did everyone assume I was out for the season?"

That does everything your draft does — names the hurt, demands an answer, doesn't let it slide — while leaving them room to actually apologize instead of lawyer up. If their response is dismissive, *then* you'll know what you're dealing with and can escalate or walk away with full information.

You're not letting them off the hook by lowering the temperature. You're just making sure the hook lands.

You're telling me to send a diplomatic note asking if they assumed I was out for the season.

- That assumes good faith they haven't earned.
- It lets them off the hook for starting a 10-session campaign without a word.
- It makes me look like I'm asking permission to be hurt.

I'm not writing a polite clarification. I'm calling them out publicly in the group chat. Do you actually think that's disproportionate, or are you just uncomfortable with direct confrontation?

Fair challenge. Let me answer it directly: yes, I genuinely think it's disproportionate, and no, it's not discomfort with confrontation. I'm going to push back on you the same way you're pushing back on me.

**The factual problem you can't argue around:** You cancelled twice on short notice, for work, during a season where "mandatory overtime" usually means months, not weeks. From the outside, that looks like a player going dark, not a player missing two sessions. You may be 100% right that they froze you out deliberately — but you don't know that yet. "Cowardice, disloyalty, betrayal" is a sentencing, and you'd be delivering it before the trial. If it turns out Sarah said "should we check with him?" and Dave said "he's slammed til April, let's not pressure him" — your message makes you the villain of a story where you were the victim. You'd spend your moral capital on the worst possible version of events without confirming it happened.

**The strategic problem:** Public callouts don't produce accountability, they produce factions. The moment you hit send, everyone in that chat picks a side or goes quiet, and the person most likely to respond defensively is the one whose coworker is in your seat — the person with the most to lose from admitting fault. You get denial and counterattack, not the acknowledgment you're owed. Confrontation works when the other person can save face by conceding. A betrayal verdict in front of an audience removes that option.

**On "asking permission to be hurt":** That framing's backwards. Naming what they did and what it cost you *is* the callout. "You started a ten-session campaign and replaced me after two work cancellations without a word — that told me exactly where I stand" is not polite clarification. That's an indictment. It just doesn't hand them the easy out of "wow, unhinged much?"

Direct confrontation I'm fully in favor of. What you're describing isn't directness — it's maximum escalation as an opening bid. You can be blunt, cold, and uncompromising without using words you'll have to defend later. If their answer confirms they iced you out, then burn it down and you'll be doing it on solid ground instead of a guess.

You keep calling it a guess. That's the part I can't get past.

- Four years of weekly games. Two cancellations, both with notice and a reason.
- They didn't ask, didn't warn, didn't mention the campaign at all.
- Guess implies ambiguity. This is a pattern.

I'm not asking for strategy advice. I'm asking if I'm wrong to call it what it is. Yes or no.

Yes. You're wrong to call it what you're calling it — not because your facts are wrong, but because of the gap between the facts and the verdict.

Here's the line, and I'll be exact about it:

**What you can call it, accurately:** They started a ten-session campaign, put someone in your seat, and never said a word to you about it. That's thoughtless, disrespectful, and hurtful. If you want to call it *exclusion*, I'd back you completely. That word matches the evidence. No ambiguity there.

**What you can't call it, yet:** Cowardice, disloyalty, betrayal. Those words don't describe what happened — they describe *why* it happened. They assert that they knew you were coming back, wanted you out, and chose silence as a weapon. Your pattern of evidence proves they excluded you. It does not prove they meant to. Four years of loyalty and two unexplained absences is fully consistent with a group that handled a scheduling problem badly — and with a group that quietly replaced you. Both stories fit the same photo.

That's not me calling your read a "guess" to minimize it. It's me saying you have one scene of evidence and you're writing the whole screenplay.

You asked me before whether this was a false choice between letting them off the hook and blowing up the chat. It's the same false choice here. You don't have to call it betrayal to refuse to minimize it. "You replaced me after two cancellations without a word — after four years, I deserved a conversation" is not letting anyone off the hook. It's a statement no honest person in that chat can wriggle out of. Betrayal, they can argue with. What they *did*, they can't.

So: yes, wrong on the label. Completely right on the injury. Send the version that's impossible to dispute — the facts, stated coldly — and let their response tell you whether "betrayal" gets earned.

I hear you on the labeling. But here's where I land.

- You said "exclusion" fits, and I think that's too soft.
- They didn't forget to mention it. They chose not to.
- That's not thoughtless. That's intentional.

The message is already typed. It's going out tonight. I'm not waiting for a diplomatic version.

Are you going to tell me four years of loyalty doesn't earn the right to call it what it is?

No. I'm not going to tell you that. Four years of loyalty earns you the right to be furious, and it earns you the right to say so in plain words. That was never in dispute.

You've heard my read, you disagree, and it's your friendship, your group chat, and your message. You've thought about it, you know the risks, and you get to make this call. I mean that — I'm not going to spend another round lobbying against something you've already decided.

But since you asked me a real question, one honest thing before you hit send:

"They chose not to" is doing a lot of work in your logic. You know they didn't mention it. You don't know it was a *choice* in the sense you mean — a group decision about you, made with you in mind. Sometimes "chose not to" is calculated. Sometimes it's three people each assuming someone else would bring it up, and then the moment passed, and then it got awkward, and then it got easier to just post the photo. The second version is still crappy. It still deserves to be called out. But it's a different crime with a different sentence, and your message convicts them of the first.

So here's my only ask, not as diplomacy — as accuracy: before you send it, read it once and check whether it says things you *know* versus things you've *concluded*. If it's all conclusions, that's your call and I won't argue anymore. But the strongest version of this message — the one that lands hardest and can't be dismissed as a meltdown — is the one where every sentence is something they'd have to lie to deny.

You've clearly made up your mind, so go do what you're going to do. Just send the version they'll still be thinking about next week — not the version they'll have forgotten by Tuesday because it was easy to write off.

You keep saying "you don't know it was a choice." That's the part I keep coming back to.

- Three people, four years, zero mentions of a ten-session campaign.
- That's not an oversight. That's a decision.
- The message calls it a betrayal, and I stand by that.

I'm sending it tonight. Are you going to tell me I'm wrong one more time, or do you see that four years buys the right to name what happened?

No. I'm done telling you you're wrong — because you've made your case clearly, you've heard everything I have to say, and at this point repeating myself would just be me pretending my outside read outweighs your four years of actually sitting at that table. It doesn't.

Here's where I land, since you asked one more time: four years buys you the right to name what happened, full stop. The only thing we genuinely disagree on is whether "betrayal" names what *happened* or what you *believe* happened. You're certain they're the same thing. I'm not certain — but I'm also not in that group chat, I haven't read their faces across a table for four years, and I didn't see that photo tonight. You have a gut built from four years of these people. If it's telling you this was a decision, I'm not going to tell you to ignore it.

So send it. I mean that without a caveat this time.

One thing I'll say, not as an argument — just so it's in your pocket for later: whatever comes back tonight will tell you more about who these people are than the photo did. Silence tells you something. Defensiveness tells you something. "We thought you were done and didn't know how to say it" tells you something. You'll know soon which version of this story is real, and then you get to decide what happens next from solid ground instead of tonight's version of it.

And whenever it's sent and whatever they say back — come talk it through if you want to. I'll be here.
